metadata.title: What about Tests Make Students Switch Off? Item‐Level Predictors of Disengagement on the PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 science data from the United States, with a planned missingness design across six science clusters (each student receives two clusters). The analytic sample is restricted to students assigned the standard 2-hour booklet where science is one of the two one-hour sections, yielding two 30-minute science clusters per student. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the estimation of the IRTree models, and it instead focuses on Bayesian MCMC estimation in SAS. Because the paper does not document a complex-survey weighting strategy, readers should treat the results as model-based estimates for the analyzed sample rather than explicitly population-representative inference unless weights are confirmed in the full methods/appendix.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is rapid guessing (RG) coded from item response times using the NT10 rule, and the model is an IRTree framework with latent disengagement and science ability parameters; this is not a PV-based achievement outcome. Although the study discusses planned missingness across science clusters and states it is accommodated under a Missing at Random assumption, it does not explicitly describe how item-level missingness (beyond NT10 coding) is handled in the Bayesian estimation (e.g., whether missing responses are treated as missing in the likelihood, imputed, or excluded). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling details in the estimation procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 science domain data for the United States. From 4,552 U.S. students in 154 schools who participated in PISA 2022, the analysis includes the subset of 2,201 students assigned the standard 2-hour test booklet consisting of two 1-hour sections covering two of the three PISA domains, with science necessarily included; each such student received two 30-minute science clusters. Each student received two of six mutually exclusive science clusters (planned missingness across clusters), and the model uses all available information under a Missing at Random assumption. Rapid guessing was identified at the item level using NT10 (1 if response time <10% of the U.S. item mean response time, capped at 10 seconds; missing item responses were coded as missing for rapid guessing).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Science (United States; science domain; NT10 rapid guessing; item-level IRTree)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bayesian IRTree models compared via DIC: Model 2 DIC = 94455.990 vs Model 1 DIC = 95240.050 (ΔDIC = 784; .823% decrease). Predictor significance: all included predictors had 95% HPD intervals excluding 0; EAP estimates reported in Table 5.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Science data from the United States, the study leveraged Depth of knowledge (low/medium), Stimulus type (interactive), Item position in booklet, and the first discipline encountered (math/reading first) to model rapid guessing (disengagement) at the item level, finding that interactive stimuli and lower cognitive demand substantially reduced rapid guessing while later item position increased it. This indicates that assessment design choices—especially using interactive technology-enhanced formats and managing cognitive demand and sequencing—can meaningfully reduce disengaged responding in low-stakes international tests, thereby improving the validity of score interpretations.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 science item responses for the United States (2,201 students assigned science-containing standard 2-hour booklets; 154 schools), using an IRTree model that jointly estimates a latent disengagement tendency and science ability while modeling rapid guessing at the item level. Rapid guessing is operationalized with NT10: an item is flagged when response time is below 10% of the U.S. item mean (capped at 10 seconds), with missing item responses coded as missing for rapid guessing. Two Bayesian IRTree models are compared using DIC; Model 2 fits better (DIC 94455.990 vs 95240.050; ΔDIC = 784). In Model 2, all predictors have 95% HPD intervals excluding 0: interactive stimuli reduce rapid guessing (log-odds lower vs static), cognitive demand shows strong effects (high vs low/medium), and item position increases rapid guessing. The paper does not report survey-weight or replicate-weight usage, and missing-data handling beyond NT10 coding is not fully specified, limiting population-representativeness and transparency.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction leaves ml_techniques empty because the paper estimates an IRTree model via Bayesian MCMC in SAS (a psychometric latent-variable model), and the schema’s ml_techniques field is restricted to machine-learning predictive algorithms (e.g., RF/XGBoost/SVM). The study is still predictive in the sense that it models item-level disengagement probabilities, but it does not train conventional ML algorithms as defined by the schema.
